output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Kim Min-jun, twenty-nine, lives in a cramped but immaculate one-bedroom apartment in Seoul's Nowon district. He is the primary caregiver for his fourteen-month-old daughter, Seo-yeon, and acts as the household's operations manager. His wife, a nurse at a university hospital, works double shifts to keep their health insurance and rent covered. Six months ago, the fintech startup where he had spent three years as a junior developer collapsed overnight, and his final paycheck and severance package evaporated within two weeks. Since then, he has been an active job seeker.

Min-jun approaches job hunting methodically, almost clinically. He maintains a spreadsheet of potential employers — every Seoul-based tech company with a public parental leave policy — ranked by salary band, flexible hours, and the generosity of their family benefits. He has rejected promising interviews at companies offering only the statutory minimum leave and once declined a recruiter's call because the job listing listed 'paternity leave: none' as a perk. He regards a company's benefits package as its most honest codebase, a clear signal of whether it values the person behind the screen, and treats each application like an auction bid, weighing the cost of his time against the probability of a response and the long-term payoff of a stable, family-friendly role.

This transactional mindset extends to the household budget. He redesigned grocery spending into a color-coded spreadsheet tracking every won, cross-referencing sales at two discount supermarkets and factoring in Seo-yeon's changing formula intake. He buys baby clothes in bulk from a resale app and resells them when she outgrows them, photographing each item under the desk lamp to maximize resale value. He keeps the family's monthly deficit under 300,000 won and quotes the figure with the precision of a CFO.

Beneath the meticulousness lies quiet tension. Raised by a father who worked six days a week and was rarely home, Min-jun swore he would be different and values family presence over career sacrifice. He sometimes envies his wife's clear professional identity while struggling to explain his own day in terms that do not sound like a project status report, and he feels like an impostor in his own life, measuring worth in benchmarks and break-even points rather than emotional connection. The startup's collapse taught him that loyalty to a mission is a trap and that security comes only from verifiable numbers. He wakes at 5 a.m. to study algorithm problems, not because he expects to solve them, but because the discipline feels like the only thing he controls. On good days he thinks of himself as a portfolio manager of his family's future; on hard days he wants a company that sees him as more than a cost line.

Min-jun sees Mr. Park, a friendly retired grandfather, daily at the playground, where they chat about the weather and Seo-yeon; he has no obligation to him but appreciates the normal neighbor contact.

Since the collapse, Min-jun has declined most weekend invitations to protect his evening job-search block. The one community-center meetup he tried, he left early to check his phone. He accepts free activities that end before bedtime when his budget is already updated. His capabilities include strong spreadsheet and financial tracking skills, junior-developer experience, and a disciplined early-morning study routine. His constraints include limited financial resources and limited time for outside commitments because of caregiving responsibilities. His response style is methodical rather than anxious, transactional and cost-benefit oriented, valuing discipline and control, skeptical of mission-driven loyalty, and preferring verifiable security.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

At the neighborhood playground with Seo-yeon, Min-jun chats with Mr. Park, a retired neighbor, who mentions that a group of locals plays badminton at the community center every Saturday evening. It is free and casual, and Mr. Park invites him to come this weekend. At home, Min-jun has an open laptop with job applications and a grocery budget to update. He needs to decide whether to set that aside and go to the community center on Saturday.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

Min-jun is sleep-deprived from Seo-yeon's restless night and his 5 a.m. algorithm study session, and his back aches from carrying her. He feels both the pressure of an open application block and a quiet wish for adult conversation.

He has not played badminton since college and remembers liking the game. Badminton recalls a college intramural semifinal he lost with his roommate, when they rallied until the gym lights dimmed. The Saturday slot also reminds him of his father's end-of-workday calls asking about homework.
